Toxocariasis.description: A zoonotic infection caused by Toxocara species, usually acquired from contaminated soil or animal feces. It typically involves migrating larvae in human tissues rather than mature adult worms in the intestine.

Anisakiasis.description: Infection caused by Anisakis larvae after ingestion of raw or undercooked marine fish or squid. Larvae can invade the stomach or intestinal wall and cause acute gastrointestinal symptoms.

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), Ri.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy causing early postural instability, axial parkinsonism, slowed movements, frontal-executive dysfunction, and a characteristic supranuclear vertical gaze palsy. MRI may show marked midbrain atrophy with relative pontine preservation (the 'hummingbird' sign).

Parkinson disease.description: A synuclein-related neurodegenerative disorder characterized by bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and later postural instability. Eye-movement abnormalities can occur, but severe early vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is unusual.

Multiple system atrophy (MSA).description: A rapidly progressive synucleinopathy with parkinsonism and/or cerebellar dysfunction accompanied by autonomic failure, such as orthostatic hypotension or urinary dysfunction.

Corticobasal syndrome.description: A neurodegenerative syndrome, often due to corticobasal degeneration or another underlying pathology, causing asymmetric parkinsonism, limb apraxia, cortical sensory deficits, dystonia, myoclonus, and cognitive impairment.

Cryptococcal meningitis (Cryptococcus ne.description: A potentially life-threatening fungal infection of the central nervous system caused most commonly by Cryptococcus neoformans, especially in people with impaired cellular immunity. The images show round budding yeasts with prominent polysaccharide capsules, characteristic of Cryptococcus.

Pulmonary cryptococcosis.description: A lung infection caused by inhalation of Cryptococcus species from the environment, which may be asymptomatic or may disseminate to the brain and other organs in susceptible individuals.

Disseminated cryptococcosis.description: Systemic infection due to Cryptococcus neoformans or Cryptococcus gattii, usually occurring in immunocompromised patients and potentially involving the lungs, central nervous system, skin, blood, bone, or other organs.

Osmotic demyelination syndrome (central.description: A noninflammatory demyelinating injury of the central pons, most often caused by rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia or other major osmotic shifts. MRI commonly shows a central pontine T2 hyperintensity with diffusion restriction, often sparing the peripheral pons.

Acute pontine ischemic infarction.description: An ischemic stroke affecting the pons, typically due to occlusion of perforating branches of the basilar artery. Acute infarcts often demonstrate restricted diffusion on MRI.

Brainstem encephalitis.description: Inflammation of the brainstem caused by infectious, autoimmune, or parainfectious processes. MRI may show T2 hyperintense brainstem lesions, sometimes with diffusion abnormalities.

Neonatal babesiosis (likely congenital B.normalized_text: Neonatal babesiosis (likely congenital Babesia microti infection)
Neonatal babesiosis (likely congenital B.description: A tick-borne or vertically transmitted protozoal infection of red blood cells. Babesia produces intraerythrocytic ring forms and characteristic tetrads (Maltese-cross forms), causing hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and systemic illness.

Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: A mosquito-borne protozoal infection in which parasites infect red blood cells. P. falciparum commonly produces multiple delicate ring forms within erythrocytes and can cause severe hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and organ dysfunction.

Congenital malaria.description: Malaria acquired transplacentally or around delivery from an infected mother. It can present in neonates with anemia, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, and parasitemia with intraerythrocytic forms.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation s.normalized_text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation secondary to severe hemolytic infection
Disseminated intravascular coagulation s.description: A systemic coagulation disorder involving excessive clotting-factor consumption and fibrinolysis, often triggered by severe infection or shock. It can produce thrombocytopenia, elevated D-dimer, and multiorgan laboratory abnormalities.

Metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma.description: An advanced prostate malignancy that can spread to pelvic lymph nodes, liver, and lungs, although bone metastases are more typical.

Metastatic neuroendocrine prostate cance.description: An aggressive subtype or transformed form of prostate cancer that often produces early visceral metastases, including liver and lung involvement.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma.description: Cancer of the colon or rectum commonly spreads first to the liver and can subsequently metastasize to the lungs.

Metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma.description: Primary liver cancer that may spread through the bloodstream to the lungs, often producing multiple pulmonary nodules.

Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis due to Gra.normalized_text: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis due to Graves disease
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis due to Gra.description: An acute intracellular shift of potassium causing severe hypokalemia and muscle weakness/paralysis in the setting of hyperthyroidism, most commonly Graves disease. Graves disease typically produces diffuse thyroid enlargement and marked hypervascularity.

Graves disease.description: An autoimmune hyperthyroid disorder caused by thyroid-stimulating antibodies, producing diffuse goiter, increased thyroid blood flow, follicular hyperplasia, and sometimes thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.

Primary hypokalemic periodic paralysis.description: A channelopathy characterized by episodic hypokalemia from potassium shift into skeletal muscle, causing acute muscle weakness or paralysis; attacks may be triggered by carbohydrate intake, rest after exercise, or stress.

Hashimoto thyroiditis with transient thy.description: An autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis that may cause thyroid enlargement and transient release of thyroid hormone; rarely, thyrotoxicosis can contribute to hypokalemic periodic paralysis.

Torus palatinus.description: A benign, noncancerous bony overgrowth arising from the midline of the hard palate; it may be smooth, nodular, or lobulated and is often asymptomatic.

Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary.normalized_text: Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary gland
Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary.description: A usually benign salivary-gland tumor that can occur on the palate, typically presenting as a slow-growing, firm, painless submucosal mass.

Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the palate.description: A salivary-gland cancer that may arise from minor salivary glands in the palate and can present as a painless swelling, sometimes with a bluish or red coloration or ulceration.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the hard pala.normalized_text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the hard palate
Squamous cell carcinoma of the hard pala.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the oral cavity that may cause an enlarging palatal lesion, often with ulceration, induration, pain, bleeding, or destructive changes.

Necrotizing sialometaplasia.description: A benign, self-limited inflammatory injury of minor salivary glands, usually affecting the posterior palate and often producing a painful ulcer that can mimic cancer.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Lumbar disc herniation at L4-L5 with cen.normalized_text: Lumbar disc herniation at L4-L5 with central spinal canal stenosis
Lumbar disc herniation at L4-L5 with cen.description: A protruding or extruded lumbar intervertebral disc can compress the thecal sac and nearby nerve roots, producing narrowing of the spinal canal. The MRI appearance is most prominent at the L4-L5 level.

Lumbar degenerative disc disease.description: Degenerative disc disease is age- or stress-related deterioration of lumbar discs, often causing disc desiccation, loss of disc height, and broad-based bulging that may contribute to back pain or nerve compression.

Lumbar spondylosis with degenerative spi.normalized_text: Lumbar spondylosis with degenerative spinal stenosis
Lumbar spondylosis with degenerative spi.description: Lumbar spondylosis refers to degenerative changes involving discs, facet joints, and supporting structures. These changes can progressively narrow the spinal canal or neural foramina and may cause neurogenic claudication or radiculopathy.

Cerebral tumor embolism from lung adenoc.normalized_text: Cerebral tumor embolism from lung adenocarcinoma
Cerebral tumor embolism from lung adenoc.description: Embolization of tumor material from a lung malignancy into cerebral arteries can cause multifocal ischemic infarcts, arterial occlusions, and sometimes hemorrhagic transformation.

Cancer-associated hypercoagulability wit.normalized_text: Cancer-associated hypercoagulability with nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis
Cancer-associated hypercoagulability wit.description: Advanced malignancy, especially adenocarcinoma, can produce a hypercoagulable state and sterile valvular thrombi, resulting in recurrent multifocal embolic ischemic strokes.

Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma.description: A rare lymphoma in which malignant lymphoid cells grow predominantly within small blood vessels, causing multifocal cerebral ischemia, hemorrhage, and variable systemic lesions.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: An inflammatory vasculitis confined to the brain and spinal cord that can cause multifocal ischemic infarcts, hemorrhage, and segmental narrowing or irregularity of cerebral arteries.

Infective endocarditis with septic cereb.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with septic cerebral emboli
Infective endocarditis with septic cereb.description: Cardiac valve infection can produce emboli causing multifocal cerebral infarctions, mycotic vascular abnormalities, and hemorrhagic lesions; pulmonary findings may occur in certain forms of endocarditis.

Sarcoidosis.description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disorder characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly involving intrathoracic lymph nodes and lungs.

Tuberculosis.description: A mycobacterial infection that can cause granulomatous inflammation in the lungs and lymph nodes, usually with caseating necrosis but occasionally with non-necrotizing granulomas.

Lymphoma.description: A malignancy of lymphocytes that commonly presents with FDG-avid mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy; granulomatous reactions may occasionally occur adjacent to lymphoma.

Osteopetrosis (adult-onset/autosomal dom.description: A hereditary osteosclerotic bone disorder caused by impaired osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, producing very dense but structurally abnormal bone and narrowing of marrow spaces.

Skeletal fluorosis.description: A chronic toxic bone disease caused by excessive fluoride exposure, leading to diffuse osteosclerosis, increased bone density, calcification of ligaments, and sometimes bone pain or stiffness.

Paget disease of bone.description: A focal disorder of accelerated and disorganized bone remodeling that can produce enlarged, sclerotic bones with coarse trabeculation, especially in the pelvis, spine, skull, and femur.

Osteoblastic skeletal metastases.description: Metastatic cancer involving bone can stimulate new bone formation, causing multifocal or diffuse sclerosis; common primary sources include prostate, breast, and some neuroendocrine tumors.

Systemic mastocytosis with skeletal oste.description: A clonal mast-cell disorder that may involve bone marrow and cause diffuse osteosclerosis, focal sclerotic lesions, osteoporosis, fractures, or mixed skeletal changes.

Germinoma intracraneal multifocal (germi.description: Un tumor de células germinales del sistema nervioso central que comúnmente afecta a la región suprasellar-hipotalámica y a la glándula pineal. La afectación supraselar puede dañar la hipófisis posterior y el hipotálamo, causando diabetes insípida central y panhipopituitarismo anterior.

Diabetes insípida central debido a afect.normalized_text: Diabetes insípida central debido a afectación hipotalámica-hipofisaria del tallo
Diabetes insípida central debido a afect.description: La secreción deficiente de hormona antidiurética (vasopresina) por hipotalámica o enfermedad hipofisaria posterior provoca incapacidad para concentrar la orina, pérdida excesiva de agua libre renal, hipernatremia e hiperosmolalidad.

Histiocitosis de células de Langerhans c.normalized_text: Histiocitosis de células de Langerhans con afectación hipotalámica-hipofisaria
Histiocitosis de células de Langerhans c.description: La histiocitosis de células de Langerhans es un trastorno histiocítico infiltrativo que puede afectar al tallo hipofisario y al hipotálamo. La diabetes insípida central es una manifestación endocrina característica, y pueden desarrollarse deficiencias hipofisarias anteriores.

Neurosarcoidosis que afecta al hipotálam.normalized_text: Neurosarcoidosis que afecta al hipotálamo y al tallo hipofisario
Neurosarcoidosis que afecta al hipotálam.description: La neurosarcoidosis es una inflamación granulomatosa del sistema nervioso que puede afectar al hipotálamo, el tallo hipofisario, las meninges y los nervios craneales. Puede causar diabetes insípida, hiperprolactinemia y panhipopituitarismo.

Linfoma primario del sistema nervioso ce.normalized_text: Linfoma primario del sistema nervioso central o linfoma secundario que afecta a la región hipotalámica-hipofisaria
Linfoma primario del sistema nervioso ce.description: El linfoma puede infiltrarse en el hipotálamo, el tallo hipofisario, la región pineal o las estructuras periventriculares y puede causar diabetes insípida central y disfunción de la hipófisis anterior.

Cor triatriatum sinister.description: A rare congenital anomaly in which a fibromuscular membrane divides the left atrium into two chambers, potentially obstructing pulmonary venous flow and producing physiology similar to mitral stenosis.

Supramitral ring.description: A congenital fibrous membrane located just above the mitral valve that obstructs left ventricular inflow and can mimic congenital mitral stenosis.

Mitral stenosis.description: Narrowing of the mitral valve that obstructs blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle, causing elevated left atrial pressure and possible left atrial enlargement.

Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.normalized_text: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency, leading to glycogen accumulation in cardiac, skeletal, and respiratory muscle. Classic infantile disease causes severe hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, and respiratory failure.

Late-onset Pompe disease.description: A milder form of acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency that primarily affects skeletal and respiratory muscles, usually presenting in childhood or adulthood with progressive proximal weakness and diaphragmatic weakness; significant infantile cardiomyopathy is uncommon.

Glycogen storage disease type III (Cori.normalized_text: Glycogen storage disease type III (Cori disease)
Glycogen storage disease type III (Cori.description: A glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency causing hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycemia, hyperlipidemia, skeletal myopathy, and sometimes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Danon disease.description: An X-linked lysosomal/autophagy-related disorder caused by LAMP2 deficiency, characterized by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, and variable intellectual disability, usually affecting males more severely.

Linfoma de Burkitt con afectación de la.normalized_text: Linfoma de Burkitt con afectación de la médula ósea
Linfoma de Burkitt con afectación de la.description: Un linfoma no Hodgkin maduro de células B altamente agresivo, generalmente caracterizado por una rápida proliferación, LDH alta, células CD19/CD10 positivas, enfermedad extranodal y posible afectación de la médula.

Linfoma difuso de células B grandes, tip.normalized_text: Linfoma difuso de células B grandes, tipo de células B en el centro germinal
Linfoma difuso de células B grandes, tip.description: El linfoma no Hodgkin agresivo más común; está compuesto por grandes células B maduras y puede afectar ganglios linfáticos, médula ósea, tejidos extranodales, hígado, bazo y tejidos blandos. Los tumores tipo centro germinal pueden expresar CD10 y CD19.

Linfoma de células B de alto grado con r.normalized_text: Linfoma de células B de alto grado con reordenaciones de MYC y BCL2 y/o BCL6
Linfoma de células B de alto grado con r.description: Un linfoma agresivo de células B maduras, anteriormente conocido como linfoma de doble impacto o triple impacto, con características clínicas y morfológicas intermedias entre el linfoma difuso de células B grandes y el linfoma de Burkitt. Comúnmente se presenta con LDH elevado, enfermedad extranodal y afectación de la médula ósea.

Leucemia/linfoma linfoblástico B-linfobl.description: Una malignidad de los linfoblastos precursores B que puede afectar a la médula ósea, la sangre, ganglios linfáticos y sitios extranodales. Comúnmente expresa CD19 y a menudo CD10, y puede causar anemia y recuentos anómalos de glóbulos blancos.

Cellulitis.description: A bacterial infection of the deeper skin and subcutaneous tissues, causing diffuse redness, warmth, swelling, and tenderness; ultrasound may show subcutaneous edema without a discrete fluid collection.

Erysipelas.description: A superficial streptococcal skin infection that produces a red, warm, swollen plaque, often with relatively well-demarcated borders and sometimes systemic symptoms.

Buttock abscess.description: A localized collection of pus in the skin or subcutaneous tissue, often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, producing painful redness, swelling, and sometimes fluctuance or drainage.

Injection-site inflammatory reaction or.description: Inflammation, cellulitis, abscess formation, or foreign-body reaction after an intramuscular or subcutaneous injection, cosmetic filler, or other local procedure.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive, potentially life-threatening infection involving fascia and deeper soft tissues. It can initially resemble cellulitis but is usually associated with severe pain, systemic illness, rapidly spreading erythema, skin necrosis, bullae, or soft-tissue gas.

Dermatomyositis.description: An inflammatory autoimmune muscle and skin disease characterized by distinctive photosensitive rashes and, often, proximal muscle weakness.

Systemic lupus erythematosus.description: A multisystem autoimmune disease that can cause photosensitive facial and chest rashes, arthritis, and other organ involvement.

Drug-induced morbilliform eruption.description: A common delayed hypersensitivity skin reaction to a medication, usually producing a symmetric widespread red maculopapular rash beginning on the trunk.

Allergic contact dermatitis or photoalle.normalized_text: Allergic contact dermatitis or photoallergic dermatitis
Allergic contact dermatitis or photoalle.description: Inflammatory dermatitis triggered by contact allergens or sunlight-associated exposures, often affecting exposed areas such as the face, neck, upper chest, and hands.

Secondary syphilis.description: A disseminated stage of syphilis that may produce a generalized maculopapular or papulosquamous rash, sometimes involving the hands and other systemic findings.

Multiple eruptive keratoacanthomas.description: A disorder characterized by the development of numerous rapidly growing keratinizing skin tumors, usually on sun-exposed or traumatized skin. Individual lesions may resemble well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma histologically.

Generalized eruptive keratoacanthoma of.description: A rare variant of eruptive keratoacanthoma characterized by widespread crops of small keratotic papules and nodules, often with ongoing formation of new lesions.

Multiple self-healing squamous epithelio.description: A rare inherited or sporadic condition causing recurrent crops of keratoacanthoma-like squamous tumors that typically enlarge and subsequently regress, often leaving scars.

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, kerat.description: A malignant keratinocyte tumor that can present as rapidly enlarging hyperkeratotic or ulcerated nodules; keratoacanthoma-type lesions may be difficult to distinguish from conventional keratoacanthoma.

Verruca vulgaris (common warts).description: Human papillomavirus-associated benign epidermal proliferations that commonly occur as rough hyperkeratotic papules on the hands and extremities and can spread through trauma-related autoinoculation.

Syringomyelia.description: A fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord, often extending over multiple spinal levels and appearing bright on T2-weighted MRI.

Hydromyelia.description: Dilation of the central canal of the spinal cord by cerebrospinal fluid; it may overlap with or represent a mild form of syringomyelia.

Chiari malformation-associated syringomy.description: A syrinx caused by impaired cerebrospinal-fluid flow at the foramen magnum, commonly associated with Chiari type I malformation and sometimes extending through the cervical and thoracic cord.

Intramedullary spinal cord tumor with as.normalized_text: Intramedullary spinal cord tumor with associated syrinx
Intramedullary spinal cord tumor with as.description: Tumors such as ependymoma or astrocytoma can obstruct cerebrospinal-fluid flow or alter cord architecture, resulting in a syrinx above or below the lesion.

B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.normalized_text: B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with IGH::IRS4 rearrangement
B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: A rare subtype of precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia characterized by marrow and blood involvement by lymphoblasts and a translocation involving Xq22.3 (IRS4) and chromosome 14q32 (IGH), often written as t(X;14)(q22.3;q32).

Precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leu.normalized_text: Precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, not otherwise specified
Precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leu.description: An aggressive hematologic malignancy caused by clonal proliferation of immature B-lymphoid precursors in bone marrow, peripheral blood, and sometimes lymph nodes or other tissues.

T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: A malignancy of immature T-lymphoid cells that can produce extensive marrow and peripheral-blood blast involvement, commonly associated with T-cell receptor gene rearrangements and sometimes a mediastinal mass.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T cells, often triggered by infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease. It produces cytokine storm, hemophagocytosis, cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, hypofibrinogenemia, and hepatosplenomegaly.

Infection-associated HLH, likely viral-t.normalized_text: Infection-associated HLH, likely viral-triggered (including severe COVID-19-associated HLH)
Infection-associated HLH, likely viral-t.description: A form of secondary HLH precipitated by a severe viral infection. Viral infections can cause diffuse pneumonitis and trigger excessive immune activation with very high ferritin, cytopenias, coagulopathy, and hemophagocytosis.

Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS).description: MAS is a secondary HLH-like hyperinflammatory syndrome, most commonly associated with systemic rheumatologic disorders such as systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis or adult-onset Still disease. It causes macrophage activation, severe cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, liver/spleen enlargement, and hypofibrinogenemia.

Primary (familial/genetic) hemophagocyti.description: A genetic disorder of impaired cytotoxic lymphocyte function that leads to recurrent or severe HLH, usually beginning in infancy or childhood but occasionally presenting later. It has the same core laboratory and histologic features as secondary HLH.

Cerebral dural arteriovenous fistula wit.normalized_text: Cerebral dural arteriovenous fistula with cortical venous reflux
Cerebral dural arteriovenous fistula wit.description: An abnormal connection between meningeal arteries and dural venous channels that causes retrograde drainage into cortical veins, producing venous congestion, dilated cortical veins, edema, and sometimes venous infarction.

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with co.normalized_text: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with cortical venous congestion
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with co.description: Thrombosis of a dural venous sinus can obstruct cerebral venous drainage, causing engorged collateral cortical veins, venous edema, hemorrhage, and venous infarction.

Isolated cortical vein thrombosis.description: Thrombosis limited to one or more cortical cerebral veins may produce focal venous congestion, swollen or hyperintense cortical veins, and adjacent cortical-subcortical edema or hemorrhagic venous infarction.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.description: A small-vessel immune-complex vasculitis characterized by IgA deposition, most often causing palpable purpura on the lower extremities and sometimes involving the gastrointestinal tract, joints, and kidneys.

Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis (h.description: An inflammatory small-vessel vasculitis of the skin, commonly triggered by medications, infections, autoimmune disease, or other immune stimuli; it typically presents with palpable purpura on dependent areas.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A systemic ANCA-associated necrotizing vasculitis that commonly affects the upper airways, lungs, kidneys, and skin. Nasal inflammation, ulceration, crusting, and epistaxis can occur.

Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis, often associated with hepatitis C infection, autoimmune disease, or lymphoproliferative disorders, causing palpable purpura and possible kidney, nerve, and joint involvement.

Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma wi.normalized_text: Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma with metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy
Oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma wi.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising in the tonsil or base of tongue/oropharynx that commonly spreads to upper cervical lymph nodes; many cases are associated with human papillomavirus (HPV).

HPV-associated tonsillar squamous cell c.description: A subtype of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, usually arising from the palatine or lingual tonsil, often presenting with a cystic or enlarged upper-neck lymph node even when the primary lesion is relatively subtle.

Cervical lymphoma involving Waldeyer rin.description: Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma can involve tonsillar lymphoid tissue and cervical lymph nodes, producing enlarged homogeneous or hypoechoic nodes and increased FDG uptake on PET imaging.

Reactive or infectious cervical lymphade.normalized_text: Reactive or infectious cervical lymphadenitis with tonsillitis
Reactive or infectious cervical lymphade.description: Inflammation of cervical lymph nodes due to infection in the tonsils, pharynx, oral cavity, or upper respiratory tract can cause nodal enlargement and increased FDG uptake.

Nested variant urothelial carcinoma of t.normalized_text: Nested variant urothelial carcinoma of the urinary bladder
Nested variant urothelial carcinoma of t.description: A rare, deceptively bland-appearing invasive variant of urothelial carcinoma characterized by small nests of urothelial tumor cells infiltrating the lamina propria or muscularis propria. It may show chromosomal abnormalities on UroVysion fluorescence in situ hybridization testing.

Conventional invasive high-grade urothel.description: The most common malignant tumor of the bladder, arising from urothelial lining cells and capable of invading the lamina propria and bladder muscle. It often has cytologic atypia, architectural disorder, and genetic abnormalities detectable by UroVysion testing.

Inverted urothelial papilloma.description: A benign urothelial neoplasm that typically forms an endophytic or inverted growth pattern composed of nests and cords of relatively bland urothelial cells. It can resemble nested urothelial carcinoma histologically, but usually lacks substantial atypia and invasive destructive growth.

Urothelial carcinoma in situ with associ.normalized_text: Urothelial carcinoma in situ with associated invasion
Urothelial carcinoma in situ with associ.description: A high-grade flat urothelial neoplasm in which markedly atypical cells involve the urothelial lining; it may coexist with invasive urothelial carcinoma elsewhere in the sampled lesion. Fluorescence in situ hybridization can demonstrate chromosomal abnormalities.

Bilateral developmental dysplasia of the.normalized_text: Bilateral developmental dysplasia of the hip with chronic subluxation/dislocation
Bilateral developmental dysplasia of the.description: A congenital or developmental abnormality in which shallow acetabula provide inadequate coverage of the femoral heads, leading to chronic hip subluxation or dislocation and secondary degenerative deformity.

Severe bilateral secondary hip osteoarth.description: Advanced degenerative joint disease caused by an underlying structural hip disorder, trauma, inflammatory disease, or chronic instability; it can produce joint-space loss, femoral-head deformity, sclerosis, and subluxation.

Bilateral femoral head osteonecrosis (av.normalized_text: Bilateral femoral head osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) with secondary collapse
Bilateral femoral head osteonecrosis (av.description: Loss of blood supply to the femoral head can cause subchondral bone death, collapse, flattening, and eventual secondary osteoarthritis. It may be bilateral, especially with corticosteroid exposure, alcohol use, sickle-cell disease, or other systemic risk factors.

Chronic inflammatory arthropathy of the.normalized_text: Chronic inflammatory arthropathy of the hips, such as rheumatoid arthritis
Chronic inflammatory arthropathy of the.description: Inflammatory arthritis can cause progressive cartilage loss, erosions, osteopenia, femoral-head destruction, and severe functional impairment; hip involvement usually occurs in established systemic disease.

Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy of the.description: A destructive arthropathy caused by impaired protective sensation, resulting in progressive joint destruction, fragmentation, subluxation, and deformity. Hip involvement is uncommon but can occur with severe neurologic disease.

Lateral patellar dislocation.description: Displacement of the patella out of the femoral trochlear groove, usually toward the lateral side; it may be acute or recurrent and is often associated with patellar instability.

Patellofemoral instability with lateral.normalized_text: Patellofemoral instability with lateral patellar subluxation
Patellofemoral instability with lateral.description: Partial lateral displacement or maltracking of the patella during knee motion without complete persistent dislocation. It commonly occurs in patients with a shallow trochlea, patella alta, or prior dislocation.

Patella alta.description: An abnormally high position of the patella relative to the femur and tibia. It can be congenital or result from patellar tendon injury and predisposes to lateral patellar instability.

Patellar tendon rupture.description: A tear of the patellar tendon causing loss of the extensor mechanism and typically producing patella alta on radiographs. This is generally an acute traumatic injury.

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A neoplasm arising from pancreatic neuroendocrine cells, often appearing as a well-circumscribed, hyperenhancing pancreatic mass. Histology commonly shows relatively uniform cells in nests, trabeculae, or sheets and neuroendocrine-marker positivity.

Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.normalized_text: Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pa.description: A rare low-grade malignant pancreatic tumor, usually occurring in young women, with solid and sometimes cystic or hemorrhagic components. Tumor cells may form solid sheets and pseudopapillary structures and often show nuclear beta-catenin expression.

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor showing acinar differentiation and production of pancreatic digestive enzymes. It often forms a large, well-demarcated solid pancreatic mass and may demonstrate acinar or sheet-like tumor architecture.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy, arising from pancreatic ductal epithelium. It is often located in the pancreatic head and may cause biliary or pancreatic duct obstruction, though some tumors can present primarily as a pancreatic mass.

Primary pancreatic lymphoma.description: A rare extranodal lymphoma involving the pancreas, usually presenting as a bulky, relatively homogeneous pancreatic mass composed histologically of diffuse lymphoid cells. Immunohistochemistry is used to establish B-cell or T-cell lineage.

Intramuscular hemangioma (venous malform.normalized_text: Intramuscular hemangioma (venous malformation) of the iliac/gluteal region
Intramuscular hemangioma (venous malform.description: A benign vascular lesion within muscle or subcutaneous tissue, often containing dilated venous channels and phleboliths; it may appear as a slowly enlarging soft-tissue mass with increased uptake on blood-pool or nuclear imaging.

Arteriovenous malformation of the pelvis.normalized_text: Arteriovenous malformation of the pelvis or gluteal region
Arteriovenous malformation of the pelvis.description: An abnormal direct communication between arteries and veins that produces a high-flow vascular nidus, enlarged feeding arteries, and early draining veins. It can cause a visible or palpable mass and superficial skin color changes.

Cavernous hemangioma of soft tissue.description: A benign lesion composed of large dilated blood-filled vascular spaces, often occurring in skeletal muscle or subcutaneous tissue and sometimes associated with phleboliths and chronic skin discoloration.

Soft-tissue angiosarcoma.description: A rare malignant tumor derived from vascular endothelial cells. It may present as a bruised, purple, or enlarging soft-tissue mass and can be hypervascular on imaging.

Knee osteoarthritis.description: Degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive loss of articular cartilage, joint-space narrowing, subchondral bone change, and osteophyte formation.

Medial compartment-predominant knee oste.description: A common pattern of knee osteoarthritis in which degeneration is greatest in the medial tibiofemoral compartment, often associated with varus alignment and increased medial load.

Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the kne.description: Degenerative arthritis developing after previous intra-articular fracture, ligament injury, meniscal injury, or other trauma that alters joint mechanics.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), s.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract, most often driven by KIT or PDGFRA mutations and typically showing spindle-cell morphology with immunoreactivity for KIT (CD117) and DOG1.

Leiomyoma.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor, commonly arising in the uterus or gastrointestinal tract, composed of bland intersecting fascicles of spindle cells and usually positive for smooth-muscle markers such as SMA, desmin, and h-caldesmon.

Leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor characterized by spindle cells, often with significant atypia, mitotic activity, and tumor necrosis; it may arise in the uterus, retroperitoneum, blood vessels, or gastrointestinal tract.

Schwannoma.description: A peripheral nerve sheath tumor composed of Schwann cells, often showing spindle-cell morphology and typically expressing S100 protein and SOX10 rather than KIT/DOG1.

SHORT syndrome (PIK3R1-related disorder).description: A rare genetic syndrome characterized by short stature, partial lipodystrophy, distinctive facial appearance, delayed teething, and insulin resistance. SHORT refers to short stature, hyperextensibility/hernia, ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, and teething delay.

Congenital generalized lipodystrophy (Be.description: A genetic lipodystrophy syndrome causing near-total absence of body fat from infancy, muscular appearance, metabolic complications including severe insulin resistance, hypertriglyceridemia, and fatty liver disease.

Russell-Silver syndrome.description: A growth-restriction syndrome typically associated with prenatal and postnatal short stature, low weight, triangular facial appearance, prominent forehead, feeding difficulty, and delayed bone maturation.

Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome (neonat.description: A rare progeroid disorder with prenatal or early postnatal growth failure, loss of subcutaneous fat, thin wrinkled skin, characteristic facial features, dental abnormalities, and apparent premature aging.
